lines.text: I told my father everything. The grain. The supply road. And the river.

Corrow's army is camped on the low meadow, on the far bank. Their supply road runs along the river, below the old Senn weir. If the weir were opened at night, the meadow would flood to the knee. The road would be mud for a week.
And how would you open a stone weir, under the eyes of two thousand men?
Quietly. With a blacksmith who knows how sluice gates work.
You read that in a book, I suppose.
Chapter fourteen. Drainage of Lowland Fields. Very dry. Excellent diagrams.
My father was quiet for a long time.
Your brother plans to charge the ford at dawn, the day after tomorrow.
Into two thousand men on solid ground? He'll lose half his knights.
Then you have one night.
We went the next night. Tobin, Wren, Oswin, twelve of ours, and Ash. No torches. No armour. Just rope, crowbars, and the dark.
The weir was guarded by four Corrow sentries, half asleep around a fire.
Four. I can drop them before they shout.
No killing, Wren. Not if we can help it.
So Ash walked out of the dark and sat down beside their fire.
All four sentries ran. I don't think they stopped until morning.
These gates haven't moved in twenty years, my lord. Rusted solid.
Then we unrust them. Together. Heave!
Twelve farmers, a knight and a blacksmith pulled on those ropes. Iron screamed. Stone cracked. And the old Senn weir opened for the first time in twenty years.
The river roared through like a living thing.
By dawn, the Corrow camp was standing in water to the knee. Tents collapsed. Wagons sank. Their supply road had vanished under a brown lake.
The meadow's flooding! Move the wagons! Move them!
And on our side of the river, the ford was narrower, shallower, and easy to hold.
What is this? Who did this? I was going to charge at dawn!
Your brother did it. With a book.
I'll never forget Maric's face. Not angry. Just confused, as if the world had stopped making sense.
I knew the feeling. I'd been having it all winter.
Corrow held out for six days, with no road and no food. On the seventh, they sent a rider with a white flag.
But across the river, behind the white flag, one figure stood apart. A woman in violet, watching our camp. Watching me.
The Lord Who Measured Zero. Chapter twelve, coming soon.
